findings.title: The global cleanup cadence is increased tenfold, not just annotation cleanup
findings.body: This ticker drives every cleanup job in the service, including dashboard-version deletion, snapshot/image cleanup, short-URL cleanup, and query-history retention/row-limit enforcement. Changing it from 10 minutes to 1 minute makes all of those database-heavy jobs run up to ten times as often; if a pass takes longer than a minute, a queued tick can also cause the next pass to start immediately. This is an unrelated operational load and lock-contention increase for a PR intended to change annotation SQL. Keep the existing cadence or schedule annotation cleanup separately/configurably.

findings.title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with every selected ID
findings.body: `err` has already been checked and is necessarily nil before this call, but the code logs the successful ID fetch at Error level and includes the complete `ids` slice. The same Error-level success logging is repeated for the delete/count and orphan-tag paths. A normal large cleanup therefore emits multiple error records containing thousands of IDs per batch, causing false alerting and potentially substantial log volume. Log successful batch progress at Debug/Info without the full ID list, and reserve Error for actual failures.

findings.title: SQLite literal ID list construction is quadratic for the large batches this change enables
findings.body: Each loop iteration formats the entire previously accumulated `values` string again (`fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`), so constructing an IN list copies an ever-growing prefix N times. This branch is used for SQLite whenever the configured batch size exceeds 999, including the newly tested 32,767-item configuration; such a batch can produce gigabytes of temporary string allocation and stall or exhaust memory during cleanup. Build the list with a pre-sized `strings.Builder` or `strconv.AppendInt` instead.
